talks.title: A New Attack Interface in Java Applications
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for A New Attack Interface in Java Applications.
talks.summary: Covers a new attack interface in java applications related to attack, interface, java.
talks.aiSummary:
Overview:
A security researcher presents an in-depth investigation into obscure attack surfaces and exploitation vectors residing within Java Database Connectivity (JDBC) drivers. By analyzing driver implementations across IBM (DB2 and Informix), MySQL, and Google Cloud Spanner, the presentation details how malicious JDBC connection parameters can be manipulated to trigger remote code execution, arbitrary file writes, SQL injection, and native library hijacking. The talk introduces novel exploitation techniques including Expression Language (EL) payloads and in-memory Bytecode Engineering Library (BCEL) web shells.

Key Topics:
- JDBC connection property abuse leading to JNDI injection (IBM DB2/Informix drivers)
- Arbitrary file write and JSP web shell planting via client trace logging configurations
- Constructing memory-only filter web shells using BCEL and Expression Language (EL) in WebLogic
- Lexical syntax and multi-byte character set exploitation in MySQL JDBC driver (setBlob with GBK)
- Unchecked class instantiation via undocumented driver properties and JNI native library hijacking

Technical Details:
The researcher systematically reviewed JDBC driver source code to identify dangerous configuration properties accepted during connection establishment. In IBM JDBC drivers, connection properties were discovered that initiate Java Naming and Directory Interface (JNDI) connections. Tracing the execution flow through internal methods—from search() into p_search(), p_result_intermediate(), c_result_intermediate_ss(), and finally c_lookup()—revealed that untrusted connection string properties trigger an outbound JNDI/LDAP lookup, providing an attacker with remote code execution.

The speaker also examined driver tracing functionality. In IBM drivers, properties such as traceFile, traceLevel, and traceFileAppend permit users to specify an arbitrary output file path and extension, allowing attackers to write client logs directly into web server directories as .jsp files. To bypass URL decoder restrictions in WebLogic Server 14 (which supports Servlet 2.4+ where Expression Language is active by default), the author crafted an EL expression payload to capture and store console administrator credentials. Furthermore, to evade disk-based detection, the speaker implemented a memory-only filter web shell: acquiring the active WebLogic thread request object, using Apache Commons Bytecode Engineering Library (BCEL) to dynamically construct and inject malicious bytecode, and registering an in-memory servlet filter for fileless command execution.

Additional attack surfaces were uncovered in lexical syntax handling and reflection. In MySQL's JDBC connector, PreparedStatement.setBlob() encloses binary streams in single quotes and escapes internal quotes and backslashes. When configured with multi-byte character sets such as GBK (unlike UTF-8 or utf8mb4), crafted byte streams within binary blob images bypass escaping logic due to character byte alignment, enabling SQL injection to execute arbitrary commands like dropping database tables. Finally, an undocumented property pluginClassName in IBM drivers (and credentialProvider in Google Cloud Spanner drivers) instantiated arbitrary classes via their no-argument constructors without validation. By specifying classes such as UnixSystem (or NTSystem on Windows), which execute System.loadLibrary("jaas_unix"), attackers who drop a malicious shared library can hijack JNI execution and achieve native code execution.

Key Takeaways:
JDBC connection URLs and properties represent a severe, unvalidated attack surface that developers often expose directly to end users. Applications must strictly sanitize and whitelist JDBC parameters, forbidding trace logging properties, custom socket factories, and classloader parameters. Database drivers should avoid dynamic class instantiation without strict type validation, and multi-byte encodings like GBK must be handled cautiously in prepared statement parsers to prevent character-escaping bypasses.

talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Alice in Kernel Land: Lessons Learned From the eBPF Rabbit Hole.

talks.aiSummary:
## Overview and Background

In the talk **"Alice in Kernel Land: Lessons Learned From the eBPF Rabbit Hole,"** researchers Valentina Palmiotti (IBM X-Force Red), Simon Scannell (Google), and Juan José (JJ) López Jaimez (Google) discuss the security architecture, threat landscape, and vulnerability research surrounding Linux's extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF). 

Modern eBPF originated as a refactor of classic Berkeley Packet Filtering (cBPF), expanding packet filtering into a general-purpose subsystem that enables user-space applications to execute code directly inside the Linux kernel without compiling or loading custom kernel modules. eBPF programs can be written in high-level languages (C, Python, Go, Rust) and compiled into eBPF bytecode. This architecture enables asynchronous execution directly in kernel space, reducing context switches between user mode and kernel mode for improved performance on modern hardware. While commonly employed for tracing, debugging, packet capturing/filtering, system call hooking, and instrumentation, the speakers note it has also increasingly been leveraged to build kernel rootkits.

---

## The eBPF Execution Model and Verification Architecture

The runtime lifecycle of an eBPF program operates through several discrete phases:

1. **Loading and Verification:** A user-mode application loads compiled eBPF bytecode into the kernel via a system call. Before execution is permitted, the kernel-side **eBPF verifier** performs static safety checks on the bytecode.
2. **Compilation and Execution:** If all verifier checks pass, the bytecode is either Just-In-Time (JIT) compiled into native machine instructions for the host architecture or executed by an in-kernel interpreter, depending on the kernel configuration.
3. **Hooking and Event Tracing:** The program is attached to a designated hook point and executes via an event-driven model triggered whenever an event occurs at that hook.
4. **Interaction via Maps and Helpers:** User-space applications and eBPF programs exchange data and communicate state using eBPF maps and kernel helper functions.

---

## Privilege Controls and Access Constraints

Access to eBPF execution is bounded by specific capability and kernel configuration settings:

* **Unprivileged eBPF:** Controlled by the `unprivileged_bpf_disabled` sysctl knob. When unprivileged access is permitted, non-root users face strict hook limitations; specifically, they are restricted to attaching programs only to sockets they own.
* **Default Distribution Hardening:** Around 2022, major Linux distributions such as Ubuntu began enabling the `CONFIG_BPF_UNPRIV_DEFAULT_OFF` kernel configuration option by default, effectively disabling unprivileged eBPF runtime access out-of-the-box via sysctl.
* **Capabilities (`CAP_BPF`):** The dedicated `CAP_BPF` Linux capability grants users or containers permission to load and run eBPF programs under relaxed constraints without requiring full administrative access (`CAP_SYS_ADMIN`). Ongoing community discussions explore restructuring capabilities further so more non-`CAP_SYS_ADMIN` workloads can utilize eBPF.
* **Lack of LSM Hooks:** eBPF currently lacks Linux Security Module (LSM) hooks, meaning it is not mediated by mandatory access control (MAC) frameworks like SELinux, preserving the necessity of dedicated eBPF security auditing.

---

## Threat Model and Attack Surfaces

The researchers define their primary threat model and auditing scope around **Local Privilege Escalation (LPE)**:

* **Target Exploitation Path:** Transitioning from an unprivileged user (or a constrained user/container possessing `CAP_BPF`) to loading an eBPF program, achieving arbitrary kernel code execution, and escalating to root privileges.
* **Practical Attack Contexts:** Environments where untrusted or semi-trusted applications process high-volume I/O and network traffic (e.g., firewall services, security monitoring tools, telemetry agents, and containerized microservices) and are granted `CAP_BPF`.
* **Out-of-Scope Surfaces:** While noting that remote code execution (RCE) is theoretically possible through bugs in packet-parsing operations or associated helper functions, the speakers focus specifically on local privilege escalation.

talks.title: Attacking the WebAssembly Compiler of WebKit
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Attacking the WebAssembly Compiler of WebKit.
talks.summary: Covers attacking the webassembly compiler of webkit related to attacking, webassembly, compiler.
talks.aiSummary:
Overview:
Security researchers Chao Zhang and Wenjun present an advanced automated fuzzing framework designed to discover vulnerabilities in WebKit's WebAssembly (Wasm) compilers within the JavaScriptCore engine. Addressing the complexity introduced by the WebAssembly 2.0 specification and the high-tier BBQ and OMG compilers, the researchers explain why traditional fuzzing techniques struggle against strict binary parsers. The speakers demonstrate a cross-engine generator migration technique that repurposes V8's mature grammar generator into an AFL++ custom mutator targeting WebKit, uncovering 13 security vulnerabilities and 4 CVEs.

Key Topics:
- WebAssembly 2.0 attack surface expansion in WebKit/JavaScriptCore (BBQ and OMG JIT compilers)
- Limitations of naive fuzzing against specification-compliant binary compiler parsers
- Cross-engine fuzzer generator extraction: decoupling V8's wasm_compile_fuzzer from libFuzzer
- Developing an AFL++ custom mutator shared library for standalone WebKit fuzzing
- WebKit performance optimizations (persistent mode, shared memory fork server) and vulnerability findings

Technical Details:
The adoption of WebAssembly 2.0 significantly expanded the WebKit codebase, with commits to the Wasm compiler surpassing those to JavaScript JIT compilers by 2022. Wasm has also emerged as a prominent browser exploitation target, highlighted by Pwn2Own 2021 Safari compromises. WebKit employs multi-tier compilation, including the BBQ (Build-Bytecode-Quick baseline JIT) and OMG (Optimizing Memory-managed Generator optimizing JIT) compilers built on the B3 and Air intermediate representation pipelines. Because JIT compilers immediately reject malformed binaries at the parser stage, generating semantically well-formed, specification-compliant Wasm modules is necessary to reach complex optimization logic.

Rather than building a grammar generator from scratch, the researchers analyzed existing implementations and determined that Google V8's wasm_compile_fuzzer was the most comprehensive and actively maintained generator. To avoid the instability and maintenance burden of porting WebKit directly into V8's codebase, the authors devised a generator extraction technique. They decoupled the generator logic from the libFuzzer target (LLVMFuzzerTestOneInput), removed the original test harness, and recompiled the V8 generator into a standalone shared library (.so) using a custom AFL compiler wrapper (afl-cc).

The resulting shared library was integrated into AFL++ as a custom mutator, allowing AFL++ mutation engines to supply random control bytes that the V8 generator transforms into valid WebAssembly binary modules wrapped in minimal JavaScript execution scaffolding. To maximize fuzzing throughput, the team implemented persistent execution mode in WebKit and enabled shared memory fork servers, increasing test execution speeds by more than 5x. When deployed on standard commodity hardware, the fuzzer surfaced crashes within 24 hours, ultimately identifying 13 unique security flaws and securing 4 CVE assignments from Apple across WebKit's BBQ and OMG compiler tiers.

Key Takeaways:
Grammar and test case generators developed for one engine contain valuable domain-specific logic that can be extracted and ported to peer implementations without architectural rewrites. Recompiling libFuzzer generators into shared libraries for use as AFL++ custom mutators enables efficient, structure-aware fuzzing against standalone target applications. Deep compiler optimization tiers (like WebKit's BBQ and OMG) require specification-compliant inputs to expose subtle code generation and intermediate representation logic bugs.

talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Breaking the Chain: An Attacker's Perspective on Supply Chain Vulnerabilities and Flaws.

talks.aiSummary:
## Overview

In this presentation, security researchers Ilay Goldman and Yakir Kadkoda from Aqua Security examine software supply chain vulnerabilities and flaws from an attacker's perspective. Drawing on their backgrounds in penetration testing and red teaming, the speakers explore how attackers target various stages of the software development lifecycle. Rather than focusing exclusively on malicious open-source packages uploaded to package managers, they emphasize mapping an organization's full attack surface from developer workstations to runtime execution.

## The Software Supply Chain Lifecycle

The speakers outline the end-to-end development flow to illustrate potential attacker entry points:

- **IDE Phase**: Where developers write code locally on their laptops.
- **SCM (Source Code Management) Phase**: Where developers and organizations store source code.
- **Registry Phase**: Platforms where organizations consume dependencies.
- **CI/CD Phase**: Systems that compile code, combine assets into artifacts, and deploy them.
- **Artifacts Phase**: Where built packages and artifacts reside, depending on whether an entity acts as a consumer or provider.
- **Runtime Phase**: Where production code and binaries are executed.

The researchers note that their original research focuses on findings across each of these phases, excluding runtime.

## IDE Phase Vulnerabilities: VS Code Marketplace Risks

The presentation examines the IDE phase in detail, focusing on Visual Studio Code:

- **Market Adoption**: Citing a Stack Overflow survey, the speakers highlight that over 74% of developers use VS Code as their primary IDE.
- **Attack Capabilities**: Extensions run directly on the developer's laptop with full user permissions. Consequently, a malicious extension can execute ransomware or steal local SSH keys to access private organization repositories on GitHub.
- **Disparity in Public Awareness**: While security research and publications frequently document malicious npm or PyPI packages, research and public reporting on malicious VS Code extensions remain minimal, often conflating vulnerable extensions with intentionally malicious ones.

## Impersonation and Typosquatting in the Marketplace

To test how easily an attacker can deceive developers, the researchers attempted to impersonate a popular extension:

- **Target Extension**: They targeted Prettier, an extension ranking in the top 10 most-installed extensions in the VS Code Marketplace.
- **Impersonation Technique**: The researchers uploaded a copy of the extension using typosquatting (`prettier` with two *t*'s).
- **Metadata Weaknesses**: While the marketplace URL contained a minor variation, the display name and publisher display name properties were completely non-unique, allowing identical display names to the legitimate extension.
- **Distinction Challenges**: The authors noted that install counts and reviews can be fabricated or manipulated, making it exceptionally difficult for developers to distinguish legitimate extensions from fraudulent copies.

talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Bypassing Anti-Cheats & Hacking Competitive Games.

talks.aiSummary:
Overview:
Bug bounty researcher and Defco Security founder Rohan (handle: nahurag) explores the ongoing technical arms race between game cheat developers and modern anti-cheat solutions in competitive PC gaming. The presentation reviews the historical progression from early user-mode protections to kernel-level anti-cheats such as Riot Vanguard and BattlEye. Rohan provides a detailed technical breakdown of internal versus external cheat architectures and demonstrates a methodology for developing ring-0 kernel cheats capable of bypassing kernel object callbacks and memory protections.

Key Topics:
- History and evolution of video game cheating and anti-cheat technologies (from Doom 2 to kernel drivers)
- Comparative architecture: Internal cheats (DLL injection) versus External cheats (standalone process)
- Anti-cheat memory protection mechanisms (ObRegisterCallbacks restricting process handles)
- Five-stage kernel cheat development lifecycle (reversing, communication, driver authoring, loading, client)
- Dynamic memory reverse engineering using Cheat Engine versus binary disassembly with IDA Pro

Technical Details:
The presentation traces game hacking from 1980s hex editing and the first 1995 Doom 2 aimbot to the early 2000s rise of multiplayer anti-cheat engines like PunkBuster and Valve Anti-Cheat (VAC). As cheat developers began executing code in kernel space, anti-cheat solutions evolved into ring-0 kernel drivers to enforce system-wide monitoring. Today, anti-cheat drivers install object notification callbacks using the Windows kernel routine ObRegisterCallbacks. When an external user-mode process attempts to obtain a handle to the protected game process via OpenProcess, the callback strips read and write privileges (PROCESS_VM_READ, PROCESS_VM_WRITE), effectively blocking user-mode cheats from reading game state or modifying memory.

To bypass ObRegisterCallbacks, cheat architectures must shift execution into the kernel. Rohan evaluates the trade-offs between internal and external cheats: internal cheats run inside the game's address space via DLL injection, offering maximum performance and flexibility but suffering from high detection rates. External cheats run in an isolated process with lower detection vectors but restricted memory access. To resolve this, external cheat clients deploy a custom kernel driver that executes arbitrary read/write memory primitives on behalf of the user-mode client.

Rohan establishes a five-stage kernel cheat development process: (1) reverse engineering game offsets, (2) establishing user-to-kernel communication via hooking, (3) authoring the kernel driver, (4) loading the driver past Driver Signature Enforcement (DSE), and (5) developing the user-mode client. Rather than analyzing obfuscated and packed game binaries in IDA Pro—which requires unpacking engine-specific structures for Unreal Engine or Unity—the author demonstrates using dynamic memory scanning in Cheat Engine. By searching for dynamic game values (such as player health) and resolving static base offsets relative to the game module's base address, cheat developers create persistent memory pointers that remain valid across Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR) and process restarts.

Key Takeaways:
Kernel-level anti-cheat defenses rely heavily on kernel handle stripping (ObRegisterCallbacks), driving modern cheat developers to operate from ring-0 kernel drivers. Relying purely on client-side or kernel-level anti-cheat drivers creates an unsustainable cat-and-mouse dynamic, as attackers consistently find methods to load unsigned or vulnerable drivers to bypass protections. Game developers must balance client-side integrity monitoring with server-side validation and anomaly detection to counteract memory manipulation.

talks.title: Dirty Bin Cache: A New Code Injection Poisoning Binary Translation Cache
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Dirty Bin Cache: A New Code Injection Poisoning Binary Translation Cache.
talks.summary: Covers dirty bin cache: a new code injection poisoning binary translation cache related to injection, code injection, dirty.
talks.aiSummary:
## Overview

Koh Nakagawa, a security researcher at FFRI Security whose primary focus includes binary translation and exploitation techniques (notably for ARM-based Windows and macOS), presents research into code injection methods targeting binary translation cache files. 

With ARM-based architectures gaining market share—projected by research data to capture 25% of the laptop market by 2027 due to long battery life—operating systems rely on translation layers to execute legacy Intel/x86 applications. Both Microsoft (via x86 emulation technologies) and Apple (via Rosetta 2) provide transparent translation layers. Because real-time translation and emulation are computationally expensive, these systems save binary translation results to disk cache files. When the same application runs again, the system reuses the cached translation rather than translating the binary twice. Nakagawa explores how an attacker can abuse these cached files to execute arbitrary code.

---

## Precursor: XDA Cache Hijacking on ARM-based Windows

Building upon previous work presented at Black Hat Europe, Nakagawa outlines the background of cache-based injection:
- **XDA Cache Files:** ARM-based Windows stores binary translation results in files named XDA cache files.
- **XDA Cache Hijacking:** By directly modifying these binary translation cache files, an attacker can perform code injection.
- **Requirements & Trade-offs:** While writing to or modifying the translation cache files requires administrative privileges, the technique offers unique side effects and benefits for an attacker, inspiring the investigation of whether similar attacks are viable against Apple's Rosetta 2 on macOS.

---

## macOS Security Architecture & the Role of Code Injection

To assess the feasibility of translating this attack to macOS, the speaker examines core macOS security constraints:
- **System Integrity Protection (SIP):** Introduced in OS X El Capitan (also called "rootless"), SIP restricts dangerous operations even from the `root` user. Root users cannot modify protected system files, delete specific binaries, load kernel extensions, or debug protected system processes.
- **Entitlements and TCC:** macOS security relies heavily on code signatures and entitlements. Privileges to access sensitive hardware or data (such as the camera, microphone, or messages) are dictated by entitlements. 
- **Code Injection Value:** Because applications are granted specific access via entitlements, injecting code into the context of an existing, trusted application allows an attacker to hijack that application's trust and inherit its entitlements, effectively bypassing privacy controls (such as TCC).
- **Hardened Runtime:** Because code injection is a primary vector for macOS exploits, the operating system strictly limits dynamic library injection and debugging by enforcing Hardened Runtime on nearly all applications. This makes finding novel code injection primitives—such as poisoning translation caches—a high-value target for bypassing macOS privacy safeguards.

---

## Rosetta 2 Internals & Installation Mechanisms

The talk examines the implementation details of Apple's Rosetta 2 translation subsystem:
- **Installation Requirements:** Rosetta 2 is not installed by default on macOS. When an Intel-based binary is executed for the first time, the system prompts the user with an installation dialog.
- **Non-Interactive / Unprivileged Installation:** Rosetta 2 can be installed via the CLI without user interaction using the `softwareupdate` command (e.g., automated execution). Installing Rosetta 2 does not require `root` privileges, allowing an unprivileged attacker to install it manually if it is not already present on the system.
- **Translation Modes:** Rosetta 2 provides two translation approaches (Ahead-Of-Time / AOT translation and Just-In-Time / JIT translation) to generate ARM64 equivalents from x86 binaries, laying the groundwork for the speaker's proposed "AOT poisoning" technique.

talks.title: Dirty Stream Attack, Turning Android Share Targets Into Attack Vectors
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Dirty Stream Attack, Turning Android Share Targets Into Attack Vectors.
talks.summary: Covers dirty stream attack, turning android share targets into attack vectors related to android, dirty, stream.
talks.aiSummary:
Overview:
Microsoft Senior Security Researcher Dimitrios Valsamaras presents research on the "Dirty Stream" attack vector, exposing how Android applications consuming shared content streams can be manipulated to execute arbitrary code. The talk examines Android inter-process communication (IPC) through ContentProviders, FileProviders, and custom share targets. Valsamaras demonstrates how consumer applications that mishandle incoming file streams and unsanitized filenames enable path traversal, arbitrary file overwriting in private app directories, and privilege escalation.

Key Topics:
- Android IPC and data sharing architecture via ContentProviders, ContentResolvers, and CursorLoaders
- Secure file sharing mechanics using FileProvider and filepaths.xml configuration mappings
- Android Share Targets and stream consumption workflows (openInputStream / openFileDescriptor)
- The Dirty Stream attack: path traversal via manipulated file metadata and DISPLAY_NAME
- Exploitation impact: overwriting application data, libraries, and achieving arbitrary code execution

Technical Details:
Android enforces strict application sandboxing by isolating each app within its own Linux user ID (UID) and private data directory, preventing direct filesystem access between packages. To facilitate controlled data sharing, the OS provides the ContentProvider framework. During application initialization in ActivityThread.main(), bindApplication() invokes installContentProviders() to register unique authority strings that identify IPC endpoints. Consumer apps query these endpoints using ContentResolver and CursorLoader to perform CRUD operations on structured data.

To share files without exposing insecure file:// URIs, applications extend androidx.core.content.FileProvider, which translates local paths into virtual content:// URIs defined in an XML configuration file (filepaths.xml). This file maps virtual aliases to device directories using tags such as <root-path>, <files-path>, <cache-path>, and <external-path>. When a consumer app receives a shared file (acting as an Android Share Target), it typically queries the provider's projection for metadata—such as MediaStore.MediaColumns.DISPLAY_NAME—and requests a file descriptor via ContentResolver.openInputStream() or openFileDescriptor() to copy the stream to local storage.

The "Dirty Stream" vulnerability arises when a consumer application naively trusts the filename returned by an untrusted content provider. A malicious application can act as a content provider or send an explicit intent containing a crafted content:// URI whose metadata includes path traversal sequences (such as ../../). When the receiving application copies the stream to its local storage, it concatenates the unsanitized display name into its private directory path (/data/data/<package>/). This enables the attacker to overwrite sensitive files—including shared preferences, SQLite databases, cached .dex files, or native .so libraries—within the victim's sandbox, leading to data exfiltration or arbitrary code execution upon application restart.

Key Takeaways:
Android developers must treat all metadata returned by external ContentProviders as untrusted input; filenames extracted from content:// URIs must be strictly validated to prevent directory traversal (../) and null byte attacks. Receiving applications should generate internal, randomized filenames when caching incoming streams rather than using caller-provided display names. Furthermore, FileProvider configurations must avoid exposing overly permissive root paths (<root-path path="." />) that grant unnecessary access to internal device storage.

(AI summary — Gemini Flash)

talks.aiSummary:
## Overview

The presentation "firmWar: An Imminent Threat to the Foundation of Computing" addresses firmware security risks within the hardware supply chain, focusing particularly on Baseboard Management Controllers (BMCs). The talk was introduced by a colleague on behalf of lead speaker Vladislav (Vlad) Babkin—a security researcher at Eclypsium with 10 years in security across CTFs, web security, and firmware—who could not attend in person due to a visa rejection. Co-author Nate Warfield, Director of Threat Research and Intelligence at Eclypsium with approximately 20 years of experience, also contributed to the research alongside the broader Eclypsium research team.

## Firmware Complexity and Supply Chain Scope

The speakers define modern firmware beyond legacy low-level boot code, emphasizing that contemporary embedded software spans numerous hardware devices:
- **PC BIOS / UEFI**: Handles machine initialization and secure boot routines, now implementing full network stacks capable of issuing outbound network requests.
- **Routers & Network Gear**: Modern enterprise routers (such as F5 routers) frequently feature substantial computing resources—often around 1 GB of RAM—and run full Linux operating system environments rather than minimal single binaries.
- **Storage Drives & Peripherals**: Hard drives run specialized firmware to manage and transfer data to storage, while IoT hardware and printers also rely on dedicated firmware environments.
- **Baseboard Management Controllers (BMCs)**: Server-grade management processors responsible for out-of-band management, power state control (power on/off), operating system installation, and hardware health monitoring.

Because of this heightened complexity, single vendors do not write all firmware components internally. Supply chain research into server components revealed that assembling a single server platform can involve up to 100 distinct organizations.

## Recurring Vulnerabilities and Code Migration

Vulnerabilities traversing hardware supply chains are historically recurring:
- **Historical Supply Chain Issues**: Traced back to instances such as catalog vulnerabilities from 2006.
- **Code Portability Issues**: The speakers highlighted a 2017 case where a vulnerability found in a car's LTE modem originated in code previously deployed in the original first-generation iPhone.
- **Compounding Risk**: When code libraries and modules are shared and migrated across different organizations, the underlying security bugs and vulnerabilities propagate with them.

## Research Findings and Zero-Day Discovery

The impetus for this specific research arose when certain hardware vendors suffered breaches and source code leaks. The researchers analyzed the leaked firmware source code and identified high-severity vulnerabilities:
- **Zero-Day Vulnerability**: Identified a previously unknown zero-day flaw (which has since become a known 1-day vulnerability).
- **Exploitation Profile**: Identified vulnerabilities that allow remote code execution (RCE).
- **Reliability**: The disclosed RCE vector is described as 100% exploitable without collateral side effects on the target system.

talks.summary: Covers forward focus - the impact of artificial intelligence related to intelligence, artificial intelligence, forward.
talks.aiSummary:
Overview:
A panel of cybersecurity experts and researchers, including Maxine Holt from Omdia and Fedor Yarochkin from Trend Micro, convenes at Black Hat to evaluate the operational realities of artificial intelligence in cyber defense and offense. The discussion cuts through industry hype to analyze the structural challenges of deploying generative models and machine learning systems in security contexts. Across the session, the panel explores data poisoning, the explainability deficit of modern neural networks, cybercrime monetization, and the widening knowledge gap between AI developers and security practitioners.

Key Topics:
- Ethical dimensions, hallucinations, and data integrity within the CIA security triad
- Cybercrime monetization of generative AI for automated black-hat SEO doorway generation
- The loss of explainability when transitioning from classical machine learning to deep learning models
- The interdisciplinary divide between AI engineers and security domain experts, alongside regulatory lag

Technical Details:
The discussion examines the fundamental requirement of data integrity when developing and operating defensive artificial intelligence systems. Maxine Holt emphasizes that within the confidentiality, integrity, and availability triad, data integrity is paramount, as corrupted or unvalidated training corpora cause large language models (LLMs) like ChatGPT to confidently output hallucinations—factually incorrect statements fabricated by the model. On the offensive side, Fedor Yarochkin points out how generative models blur the boundary between benign automation and malicious activity. ## Overview

In this talk, freelance penetration tester Linus Kvarnhammar details his work on the Swedish public television (SVT) series *Häckad* (*Hacked*). The six-episode show was designed to raise cybersecurity awareness among regular citizens by demonstrating how real-world attackers compromise devices and personal accounts. Production was constrained to a strict budget of three days per episode to conduct both the hacking assessments and the filming, supported by team members David Jacoby and Jesper Larsson. Kvarnhammar shares the technical and social engineering methodologies used during the episode targeting everyday individuals.

## Participant Selection and Casting Pretext

To simulate consumer-targeted attacks:
* **Recruitment Pretext:** SVT recruited participants via a Facebook group under the guise of an intentionally vague "digital experiment."
* **Logistics & Staging:** During COVID-19 restrictions, 20 applicants were invited to an in-person casting call and split into groups of five.
* **Insider Plant:** In each group of five, the fifth person was covertly team hacker Jesper, who acted as an inside social engineering agent to steer the targets.

The team established a mock hacking office and executed multiple coordinated attack vectors:

* **Fake Portal & Credential Harvesting:**
  * Targets were instructed to fill out an onboarding form on a specially crafted website named "digital experiment."
  * The portal provided credential harvesting options, including fake Single Sign-On (SSO) login pages mimicking Facebook, Google, and LinkedIn, as well as native account registration where participants reused passwords.
* **Credential Leak Databases:**
  * The team queried public breach and leak databases using the participants' email addresses to cross-reference reused passwords.
* **Social Engineering & Malicious USB Drops:**
  * When users completed the web form, an intentional error message was displayed.
  * Jesper claimed to have encountered the identical error and handed targets a malicious USB flash drive containing weaponized PDF files intended to fix the problem.
* **Backdoor Delivery:**
  * The USB drives carried trojanized PDF backdoors for both Windows and macOS.
  * While the Windows payload failed to execute properly due to a build flaw, the macOS backdoors operated successfully, compromising all 7 participants who brought Mac computers.
* **Outcome:**
  * The team compromised usernames and passwords for all 20 participants, obtaining multiple credentials for several targets.

After gathering credentials and backdoor access from the initial pool, the team selected two participants who were well-suited for television, focusing particularly on a participant named Frida:
* **Host and Account Access:** The team maintained full remote access to Frida's Mac and several of her online accounts.

Overview:
Sandro Pinto, an associate research professor at the University of Minho, alongside PhD researcher Cristiano, presents research challenging the long-standing belief that microcontrollers (MCUs) are immune to microarchitectural timing attacks. While microarchitectural attacks like Spectre and Meltdown have focused on complex application processors, the speakers demonstrate that timing side channels exist on resource-constrained embedded systems. The talk details the "Busted" attack, which exploits MCU bus interconnect contention to extract cryptographic secrets across hardware security boundaries.

Key Topics:
- Architectural differences between complex application processors (APUs) and resource-constrained microcontrollers (MCUs)
- Bus interconnect arbitration logic as a novel hardware microarchitectural timing side channel
- Constructing "Smart Gadget Networks" from autonomous hardware peripherals to bypass single-core limitations
- The "Busted" attack against Arm Cortex-M33 TrustZone-M extracting SmartLock PINs in real time

Technical Details:
The researchers highlight the architectural disparity between high-performance application processor units (APUs) like Intel Skylake—which utilize multi-level caches, 10-19 stage pipelines, branch predictors, out-of-order execution, and virtual memory—and microcontrollers (MCUs) such as Arm Cortex-M devices. MCUs typically feature in-order execution, short 2-3 stage pipelines, physical addressing only, and run real-time operating systems like Zephyr. Because MCUs lack complex caches and speculative execution units, the security community largely assumed that microarchitectural timing attacks were impractical on embedded hardware.

The speakers invalidate this assumption by identifying the MCU bus interconnect arbitration logic as an unmitigated timing side channel. In an MCU, multiple bus masters—such as the CPU core and Direct Memory Access (DMA) controllers—share access to memory banks and slave peripheral ports (e.g., UART, I2C, SPI, and CAN). When simultaneous bus transactions target the same memory bank or port, the bus arbiter stalls one of the transactions. However, because MCUs typically contain only a single CPU core, attackers cannot execute concurrent software spy threads alongside victim execution. To bypass this constraint, the authors introduce "Hardware Gadgets" that link autonomous on-chip peripherals into a "Smart Gadget Network," enabling automated, background memory contention without CPU intervention.

To demonstrate practical exploitation, the researchers implement the "Busted" attack on a state-of-the-art Armv8-M Cortex-M33 microcontroller utilizing TrustZone-M hardware isolation. Target modeling simulates an IoT SmartLock application using manufacturer reference code for a trusted keypad. By generating background memory bus contention via the Smart Gadget Network while the secure keypad application runs, the unprivileged Non-Secure world monitors bus arbitration timing differentials. This allows the attack to bypass TrustZone isolation and reconstruct the user's secret PIN in real time.

Key Takeaways:
Embedded systems engineers and hardware designers must recognize that simple, cacheless MCUs are vulnerable to microarchitectural timing side channels through bus arbitration contention. Hardware isolation mechanisms like Arm TrustZone-M do not inherently protect against timing leaks caused by shared memory buses and concurrent peripheral operations. Defensive designs must implement deterministic bus arbitration schemes, partition memory banks between secure and non-secure masters, and monitor autonomous DMA transfers.

## Overview

In this presentation, Antoine Vastel and Konstantina Kontoudi (Lead Data Scientist) from DataDome discuss detecting distributed bad bot attacks without relying on traditional CAPTCHAs. While CAPTCHAs are widely deployed to challenge automated traffic, they create poor human user experiences and are increasingly circumvented by CAPTCHA-solving farms as well as image and audio recognition algorithms. To counter this, the speakers present an approach combining streaming-based outlier detection with SliceLine, a machine learning technique designed to identify distributed bot activity.

---

## Bot Motivations and Tooling

Bots are automated programs capable of executing tasks for benign applications (such as automated site testing or web indexing by Googlebot) or malicious operations. Malicious use cases highlighted include:

- **Credential Stuffing:** Attempting automated logins using batches of stolen credentials to take over user accounts.
- **DDoS Attacks:** Flooding sites or mobile applications to degrade performance or cause complete unavailability.
- **Credit Card Testing:** Validating stolen card batches to verify active status before reselling them at higher rates.
- **Metric Manipulation:** Artificially inflating views, retweets, and engagement counters.

Attackers implement bots using two primary architectures:
1. **Simple HTTP Clients:** Built with language libraries such as `axios` (Node.js) or `aiohttp` and `requests` (Python). These require low CPU and RAM resources but do not execute JavaScript natively, often exposing inconsistent HTTP headers or TLS fingerprints.
2. **Automated / Headless Browsers:** Built with frameworks such as Puppeteer, Playwright, or Selenium automating Chrome. While computationally expensive, they run full JavaScript engines, support native browser APIs, and generate consistent HTTPS/TLS signatures.

---

## Detection Signals and Bypass Challenges

Bot mitigation architectures evaluate multiple signal categories across rules and machine learning pipelines:

- **Signatures and Fingerprinting:** Collecting HTTP headers, TLS fingerprints, and TCP fingerprints on the server side, alongside browser-level JavaScript fingerprints on the client side.
- **Behavioral Analysis:** Tracking mouse trajectories, typing cadence, and client/server interaction flows (e.g., flagging abnormal sequences such as adding an item to a cart before viewing the product page).
- **Reputation Signals:** Scoring IP addresses, sessions, and proxy infrastructure based on historical abuse.
- **Contextual Signals:** Correlating request origins, geolocation, and timestamps against expected target traffic baselines.

Detection can leverage tool-specific artifacts—for instance, default Selenium ChromeDriver executions leave a detectable `document.$cdc_` property in the DOM. However, attackers regularly attempt to bypass detection by spoofing client-side properties, altering JavaScript fingerprint attributes, and manipulating request headers.

---

## Distributed Attacks and Outlier Detection

To overcome simple rate-limiting and signature-based blocking, bot operators distribute malicious traffic across thousands of residential proxies and IPs, rotating identities and forging signatures. Because client-side indicators can be altered or forged, the defense strategy focuses on analyzing real-time traffic distributions via streaming-based outlier detection coupled with SliceLine. This approach identifies anomalous multidimensional slices of traffic across high-dimensional features where distributed bot campaigns subtly diverge from baseline human behavior.

Jos Wetzels, a security researcher with Forescout, analyzes downstream lateral movement and post-exploitation strategies targeting Purdue Level 1 control devices in operational technology (OT) environments. While industrial security research traditionally focuses on IT/OT boundary hopping or upstream attacks against SCADA systems, this talk explores the unseen "Nakatomi space"—the unmonitored network crawl spaces beneath Level 2. Wetzels details how attackers exploit multi-homed Level 1 PLCs, nested fieldbus networks, safety system integrations, and third-party packaged units to compromise critical infrastructure.

- Purdue Model architecture and lateral movement dynamics at Level 1 (PLCs, RTUs, nested networks)
- The concept of "Nakatomi space": Unmonitored OT network crawl spaces across fieldbuses, serial links, and proprietary RF
- Exploiting multi-homed Level 1 devices across unacknowledged perimeters

Technical Details:
Industrial automation environments adhere to the Purdue model, where Level 2 hosts local HMIs, SCADA servers, and engineering workstations, while Level 1 hosts control devices like Programmable Logic Controllers (PLCs) and Remote Terminal Units (RTUs). Traditional security assessments concentrate on boundary segmentation between IT and OT or lower-level devices hacking upstream into SCADA. Wetzels explores downstream and east-west movement within Level 1, termed "Nakatomi space"—analogous to moving through the building ducts in the film Die Hard. These environments encompass non-routable fieldbuses (Profibus, Profinet, CANopen), industrial wireless (WirelessHART, proprietary 900 MHz RF, TETRA), and serial point-to-point links that operate entirely outside the visibility of network intrusion detection systems.

When attackers achieve code execution on Level 1 PLCs, multi-homed devices become unacknowledged perimeter gateways. A key target of lateral movement is the integration between the Basic Process Control System (BPCS) and the Safety Instrumented System (SIS). While historically air-gapped, modern plants connect them via Level 2 firewalls or direct, non-routable point-to-point serial or Ethernet links. An attacker pivoting from a compromised BPCS PLC can abuse legitimate safety bypass mechanisms. Safety functions are routinely bypassed during startup, phase transitions, or maintenance using HMI activation signals. Attackers targeting these interfaces work to circumvent physical enablement switches and software timeouts, allowing them to permanently disable safety shutdown mechanisms and prevent automated responses during an industrial attack.

Wetzels also highlights the risk posed by third-party "packaged units"—self-contained black-box control systems for specialized functions such as HVAC, chemical injection, water treatment, or gas turbines. Asset owners often have no administrative visibility into these units, which are frequently equipped with cellular or wireless modems for vendor remote maintenance. Packaged units interface with the core plant network through fieldbus couplers, which act as rudimentary gateways mapping input and output memory ranges. Compromising vendor remote maintenance connections allows attackers to traverse these fieldbus couplers and penetrate core Level 1 networks without passing through enterprise perimeter controls.

Key Takeaways:
OT asset owners must identify and inventory multi-homed Level 1 devices, serial connections, and fieldbus couplers as functional security perimeters. Organizations must isolate Safety Instrumented Systems from BPCS networks to prevent unauthorized activation of safety bypasses. Visibility and network monitoring tools must be extended beyond Ethernet to inspect industrial fieldbuses, serial links, and vendor remote maintenance connections.

## Overview

Presented by Xiang Li (Charlie), a PhD student from Tsinghua University, this talk introduces the **Phoenix Domain Attack** (published at NDSS 2023). The attack represents a novel DNS cache injection technique that allows revoked or expired domain names to remain continuously resolvable on vulnerable recursive resolvers at scale. 

Domain names serve as core infrastructure for services like web hosting, CDNs, email, and certificates, with Verisign reports noting approximately 350 million registered domains. However, domains are frequently abused for cybercrime such as botnet command-and-control, phishing, and malware distribution (with reports from March 2023 identifying over 620,000 domains exhibiting security threats). To counter this abuse, registries and registrars implement domain revocation by deleting domain name server (NS) records from Top-Level Domain (TLD) zone files or redirecting nameservers to security sinkholes. The Phoenix Domain Attack breaks this defense mechanism, allowing adversaries to evade domain takedowns and keep malicious domains alive.

---

## Background: The Ghost Domain Attack and Past Fixes

The Phoenix Domain Attack builds upon the foundational concept of the **Ghost Domain Attack**, which was originally discovered and proposed by the speaker's lab in 2012:

- **Mechanics of Ghost Domain**: Prior to domain revocation (e.g., of `botnet.com`), an attacker queries a target recursive resolver to populate its cache with the attacker’s NS records. Once the TLD registry removes the delegation records from the TLD zone file, non-cached resolvers cannot resolve the domain. However, before the cached NS record's Time-To-Live (TTL) expires on the target resolver, the attacker queries their own domain again. Exploiting implementation flaws in resolvers, the attacker returns a new NS record with a larger TTL and higher trust level, repeatedly refreshing the cache and keeping the revoked domain alive indefinitely.
- **Historic Mitigations**: Ghost Domain impacted major DNS software implementations, including BIND and PowerDNS. Vendors mitigated the vulnerability by enforcing strict rules that prevent recursive resolvers from prolonging or refreshing TTL values beyond the original expiry window, ensuring cached records eventually expire as intended.

---

## The Phoenix Domain Attack

A decade after the Ghost Domain vulnerabilities were addressed, researchers investigated whether domain revocation guarantees held across modern DNS ecosystems. They found that domain revocation remains broken due to broader, protocol-level weaknesses:

- **Core Impact**: The Phoenix Domain Attack enables an attacker to keep revoked domains resolvable across target recursive resolvers for free, even after domains expire or are deleted from TLD zone files.
- **Protocol-Level Scope**: Unlike Ghost Domain, which primarily exploited implementation bugs in specific resolver software, Phoenix Domain targets deeper vulnerabilities in DNS delegation, revocation, and protocol interactions (such as DNSSEC / DS record behaviors).
- **Attack Variants**: The research identified two distinct variations of the attack, designated as **T1** and **T2**, which operate across a broader attack surface to bypass traditional TTL renewal restrictions and maintain continuous domain resolution.

Overview:
Taeyoung Chen, a PhD researcher from the University of Birmingham, presents PMFault, an attack demonstrating software-controlled voltage fault injection on server platforms via the Power Management Bus (PMBus). Building upon previous research like Plundervolt and hardware-based bus modification, Chen shows how server-grade motherboards can be manipulated without opening the chassis. The presentation explores the voltage regulation circuitry of modern servers, detailing how onboard management controllers can be leveraged to inject faults into cryptographic operations within Intel SGX enclaves.

Key Topics:
- Evolution of voltage fault injection: From Plundervolt software interfaces to hardware SVID bus modding and PMBus exploitation
- Supermicro X11 server motherboard architecture and MPS MP2955/MP2965 voltage regulators
- Scanning and interacting with PMBus devices over I2C using i2c-tools to discover voltage control registers
- Achieving recoverable CPU stalls and remote fault injection against Intel SGX via Baseboard Management Controllers (BMCs)

Technical Details:
Chen examines the progression of voltage fault injection attacks, beginning with Plundervolt (CVE-2019-11157), which exploited Intel MSR 0x150 to undervolt the CPU from software and induce computational errors in algorithms like AES-NI and RSA-CRT. After Intel mitigated Plundervolt through microcode and BIOS updates that locked the voltage configuration interface, physical hardware attacks emerged targeting the Serial Voltage Identification (SVID) bus between microcontrollers and voltage regulators on desktop boards. Chen investigates whether server platforms remain vulnerable by analyzing a Supermicro X11 server motherboard equipped with a Monolithic Power Systems MP2955 voltage regulator (referencing the pin-compatible MP2965 datasheet).

Analysis of the voltage regulator revealed dedicated SCL and SDA pins running the Power Management Bus (PMBus)—an I2C-based protocol with standardized and vendor-specific command sets. By executing i2c-tools (i2cdetect) from the host CPU, the researchers scanned the bus and enumerated 12 connected devices. Using heuristics—specifically querying the READ_VOUT command to match expected idle voltages below 0.55V and checking the PMBus address register—they located the target voltage regulator at hex address 0x20. While sending PMBus undervolting commands directly from the CPU caused immediate system stalls, testing with a Raspberry Pi established that these stalls were fully recoverable: temporarily dropping the voltage and immediately restoring nominal levels allowed the processor to resume execution, providing the exact timing loop necessary for fault injection.

To convert this technique into a practical attack that complies with the Intel SGX threat model (which excludes physical chassis intrusion), Chen examined the server's Baseboard Management Controller (BMC). On server motherboards, the BMC is directly hardwired to the PMBus for environmental and thermal telemetry. Furthermore, the BMC possesses a dedicated management Ethernet interface, shares an Ethernet interface with the host, and links directly to the host CPU via the Keyboard Controller Style (KCS) interface. By executing commands through the BMC, an attacker can programmatically undervolt the CPU through PMBus, inducing faults in SGX enclave operations entirely across network and software boundaries.

Key Takeaways:
Server motherboard management buses such as PMBus and I2C introduce critical hardware attack surfaces that enable remote physical-layer fault injection. Locking processor-level undervolting registers (such as MSR 0x150) is insufficient when peripheral controllers retain unrestricted write access to voltage regulators. Hardware vendors must enforce strict access controls on PMBus commands, validate voltage regulator firmware, and isolate BMC interfaces and KCS channels from untrusted execution contexts.

Overview:
Elastic principal security researcher Gabriel Landau details the security architecture and attack evolution surrounding Windows Protected Process Light (PPL). After analyzing historical user-mode and kernel-mode PPL bypasses—and Microsoft's mitigations against original attacks like PPLdump—Landau introduces a novel user-mode vulnerability chain named "PPLfault." The presentation details how an administrative attacker can abuse opportunistic locks, loopback SMB, memory manager paging behavior, and the Windows Cloud Filter API to execute arbitrary code within PPL processes without kernel drivers.

Key Topics:
- Windows Protected Process Light (PPL) architecture, signer levels, and access restriction primitives.
- Historical bypasses: KnownDlls hijacking, ELAM driver intermediate CA abuse, and kernel mode PreviousMode manipulation.
- Design and mechanics of the novel "PPLfault" exploitation technique.
- Opportunistic locks (oplocks), loopback SMB, and Cloud Filter API (`cldapi.dll`) rehydration callbacks.

Technical Details:
Protected Process Light (PPL) was engineered to defend critical system processes (such as `lsass.exe` via RunAsPPL) and endpoint security engines from user-mode tampering. By enforcing signature verification (requiring Antimalware or Windows signer levels) and stripping intrusive rights from process handles (such as `PROCESS_VM_READ`, `PROCESS_TERMINATE`, and `PROCESS_DUP_HANDLE`), PPL blocks standard credential dumping and injection techniques. Historical exploits like Clément Labro's PPLdump abused object manager directory symlinks and `DefineDosDevice` to manipulate the `\KnownDlls` cache. Microsoft countered these attacks by implementing low-privilege process trust labels on object manager namespaces, neutralizing arbitrary symbolic linking into KnownDlls.

Landau explores existing bypass alternatives, including abusing overly permissive Early Launch Anti-Malware (ELAM) drivers (via tools like `antimalware-blight`) to launch arbitrary processes as Antimalware-Light, and kernel exploitation primitives (such as Angry Orchard) that overwrite `KTHREAD.PreviousMode` from UserMode (1) to KernelMode (0) to grant unrestricted system handle access. He then unveils "PPLfault," a purely user-mode exploitation chain that defeats PPL integrity enforcement. PPL relies on 4KB page hashes embedded within file digital signatures, verifying individual memory pages as they fault in from disk.

PPLfault exploits this paging mechanism by leveraging the Windows Cloud Filter API (`cldapi.dll`) to construct an empty placeholder file associated with a controlled user-mode rehydration callback. The attacker maps a target DLL (such as `EventAggregation.dll` loaded by `services.exe`) through loopback SMB (`\\127.0.0.1\...`), which permits placing opportunistic locks (oplocks) on executable image files. When the PPL process attempts to map and execute the library, the oplock breaks. The exploit leverages `SeProfileSingleProcessPrivilege` to flush the system working set and standby list, forcing memory pages out to disk. During subsequent page fault resolution, the Cloud Filter rehydration callback intercepts the memory request, allowing the attacker to manipulate memory contents and gain arbitrary code execution inside the PPL process.

Key Takeaways:
Windows Protected Process Light remains susceptible to complex user-mode architectural abuse that exploits file system minifilters, loopback networking, and memory manager page faulting. Relying strictly on signature levels and page hashes is insufficient when underlying file system abstractions permit out-of-band data manipulation during paging. To counter PPLfault, Landau released "NoFault," an open-source driver that programmatically enforces the `ImageLoadNoRemoteImages` mitigation option on PPL binaries early in their lifecycle, preventing execution over SMB shares.

## Overview

In this presentation, Sarah Young, a Cloud Security Advocate at Microsoft based in Melbourne, discusses the challenges surrounding security content creation and advocacy. Drawing from her background in writing Microsoft certification exam books, hosting a Microsoft-focused podcast, and conducting independent research, Young highlights how security advocacy often targets the wrong audience. While technical subjects like Java or .NET primarily concern niche developer audiences, cybersecurity uniquely impacts everyone who connects devices or systems to the internet—spanning security specialists, general IT professionals, and everyday users.

## The Echo Chamber in Security Content

Young observes that security professionals predominantly produce technical content aimed solely at other security professionals. When creating new material, authors routinely send drafts to peers and teammates within the security domain for feedback. While these internal reviewers typically validate the work positively, creators fail to evaluate whether the material is understandable, accessible, or practically useful for the wider non-security community.

## Content Proliferation and Quality Challenges

The barrier to entry for content production has fallen significantly with the growth of the internet and online platforms. Anyone can easily purchase a microphone or publish material across a wide variety of consumable media formats:
- Documentation and guides
- Training materials and courses
- Videos and podcasts
- Blog posts

While this accessibility democratizes publishing, it introduces quality control issues. Because much of this output is self-published, completely unvetted, and unreviewed by external audiences, the overall quality and pedagogical value of security guidance remains inconsistent.

## Defining Content Creators in Tech

Young addresses common perceptions of "content creators," noting that while people frequently picture mainstream social media figures (such as YouTube influencer PewDiePie), technical creators exist across multiple categories:
- Professional advocates and developer relations (DevRel) personnel whose core responsibility is educational content creation.
- Technical practitioners, engineers, and everyday security specialists who independently publish blogs, guides, and consumable media.

Overview:
Mathy Vanhoef and collaborators from KU Leuven present new offensive research examining security vulnerabilities in Wi-Fi access point implementations, focusing on the abuse of sleep mode and power-save buffering mechanisms in WPA2 and WPA3 networks. Building on the foundational concepts of the KrØØk vulnerability, the authors analyze how access points manage client security contexts and buffered frames across state transitions. They demonstrate practical attacks that bypass client isolation to intercept sensitive traffic, subvert 802.11w Management Frame Protection (MFP) to disconnect legitimate clients, and manipulate Fine Timing Measurement (FTM) distance calculations.

Key Topics:
- Wi-Fi power-save buffering flaws and security context switching (building on KrØØk)
- Client isolation bypass and traffic interception via MAC address spoofing and key overwriting
- Bypassing 802.11w Management Frame Protection (MFP) in WPA3 via sleep-mode Association Requests
- Access point kernel vs. user-space race conditions in Security Association (SA) Query handling and FTM manipulation

Technical Details:
The researchers explore how access points buffer outbound frames when channels are congested or clients enter power-save sleep states. Building upon KrØØk—where disassociation frames caused APs to clear encryption keys while mistakenly transmitting buffered frames in plaintext—the speakers investigated whether buffered frames could be transmitted under an attacker-controlled security context. In shared Wi-Fi environments implementing client isolation (such as eduroam or Hotspot 2.0), an authenticated attacker sniffs the victim's MAC address and monitors outbound requests, such as DNS or HTTP queries forwarded to the internet. Before the external response returns, the attacker spoofs the victim's MAC address and connects using attacker credentials. This overwrites the AP's internal mapping, binding the victim's MAC to the attacker's newly negotiated session key. When the returning response arrives, the AP encrypts the pending frame using the attacker's session key and transmits it directly to the attacker, completely bypassing client isolation.

The authors also demonstrate how sleep-mode signaling weaponizes denial of service against WPA3 networks protected by 802.11w Management Frame Protection (MFP). Under standard operations, spoofed management frames trigger an SA Query procedure to verify if the original client is active. However, an attacker can transmit an unauthenticated Association Request with the power-management sleep bit asserted. While the user-space daemon queues an SA Query to confirm client presence, the kernel notes the reported sleep state and buffers the query frame indefinitely. Because the client never receives the query, the user-space daemon times out awaiting a response, assumes the client disconnected, and tears down the legitimate connection. Furthermore, abusing sleep-mode signaling skews 802.11 Fine Timing Measurement (FTM) distance calculations used in location tracking and geofencing.

Key Takeaways:
To defend against context-overwriting interception, access points must prevent recently active MAC addresses from immediately reconnecting under different security contexts, and administrators should segment untrusted clients into separate VLANs. To mitigate WPA3 denial-of-service, access point firmware must never buffer SA Query management frames, transmitting them immediately regardless of reported sleep states. In addition, IEEE 802.11 standards must be updated to cryptographically authenticate power-management control bits. The authors developed an open-source dual-adapter testing tool to audit networks for these vulnerabilities, noting that while most vendors remained vulnerable, Ubiquiti had deployed functional mitigations.

## Overview

The presentation "The Various Shades of Supply Chain: SBOM, N-Days and Zero Trust" is delivered by Kai Michaelis (CTO at immune, focusing on firmware security), Alex Matrosov (Binarly, leading the offensive research), and Richard Hughes (Red Hat, maintainer of the Linux Vendor Firmware Service [LVFS] and fwupd). The talk focuses on firmware security mechanisms in real-world UEFI implementations, recent attacker behaviors, and the unique structural challenges inherent to the firmware supply chain compared to traditional software ecosystems.

## Firmware Supply Chain Complexity and Implicit Trust

Unlike conventional operating system software, laptop and server firmware does not originate solely from device OEMs like Dell or Lenovo. Instead, the pipeline involves multiple tiers of handoffs:

- **Silicon Vendors:** Produce initial reference code and reference implementations.
- **Independent BIOS Vendors (IBVs):** Add proprietary software stacks and features.
- **Original Design Manufacturers (ODMs):** Assemble and package various third-party firmware components, sign the resulting images, and forward them to the OEM.
- **Original Equipment Manufacturers (OEMs):** Brand the system and distribute it to end customers and data centers.

Because binaries are collected and integrated from various sub-tier suppliers and subcontractors without standardized verification at each stage, the entire chain relies heavily on implicit trust.

## The N-Day Vulnerability Recurrence Problem

A major consequence of this multi-tiered handoff model is the persistent reintroduction of known vulnerabilities ("N-days"). The speakers highlight the USB-RT vulnerability as a prime example:

- **2016:** The USB-RT vulnerability was first discovered and patched.
- **2017:** The exact same vulnerability was rediscovered in shipped products because an entity in the supply chain used older, unpatched reference code.
- **2020–2022:** The vulnerability resurfaced repeatedly across multiple releases; in 2022 alone, three different vendors shipped vulnerable reference code due to broken communication channels and fragmented update distribution.

Because critical security notices fail to propagate reliably across all participants, downstream binaries frequently carry known security flaws into production hardware.

## Applying Zero Trust and Continuous Verification to Firmware

To counter implicit trust assumptions, the speakers advocate adapting networking Zero Trust concepts to the firmware domain:

- **Minimizing Trust Assumptions:** Treat internal firmware components as untrusted by default, requiring explicit verification regardless of the source.
- **Continuous Binary Verification:** Firmware must not be validated merely once during initial assembly. Because update packages are often assembled by different teams or suppliers who may fail to include prior patches, verification must occur continuously across the entire firmware update lifecycle.
- **Transparency Hierarchy:** A structured approach to trust where the ideal state is open-source software built using reproducible builds. Reproducibility enables defenders to audit the underlying source code and deterministically verify that the resulting binary matches the audited code.

Overview:
A panel of Black Hat Asia review board members—including Asuka from Elastic, Sudhanshu from Red Hunt Labs, Pamela from Shea Security, and Tai from threatintel.com, moderated by Jeff—discusses prominent themes and technical takeaways from the conference. The panelists critique industry hype surrounding generative AI and large language models, contrasting marketing buzz with practical automation needs in Security Operations Centers (SOCs). The conversation highlights the irreplaceable value of human analytical intuition in bug hunting, the hidden workforce powering AI, and the persistent recurrence of basic security hygiene failures.

Key Topics:
- Generative AI hype versus practical automation in SOC environments (alert triage and log reduction)
- Logic flaws versus memory corruption: The necessity of human intuition in vulnerability discovery
- The hidden human workforce behind commercial AI models (data annotation, content moderation, RLHF)
- Fundamental cybersecurity deficits: Asset visibility, credential hygiene, and workforce development

Technical Details:
The panel opens by addressing the widespread fascination with generative AI and large language models like ChatGPT. The panelists caution that the security industry is treating AI as a universal buzzword—drawing parallels to past hype cycles around blockchain. In practical defensive operations, the most valuable application of machine learning is not generative text generation, but high-volume automation and log analysis. SOC Level-1 analysts suffer from severe alert fatigue and burnout; effective machine learning applications should focus on filtering out up to 90% of redundant SIEM alerts and identifying anomalous patterns within large telemetry datasets, freeing analysts from repetitive manual log reviews.

In offensive security and vulnerability research, panelists reference two conference presentations: research on fuzzing the Linux packet filter and an Android proof-of-concept chaining two vulnerabilities. In both cases, researchers achieved breakthroughs by manually identifying complex business and architectural logic flaws rather than relying purely on automated fuzzing tools hunting for raw memory corruption. The panel draws an analogy to NASA's HARP citizen science project, where human volunteers listening to and visually analyzing solar wind plasma waveforms consistently outperform AI models. Automated tools excel at processing scale, but human creativity remains essential for identifying contextual and logic-based vulnerabilities.

The discussion also addresses systemic workforce challenges and the reality behind commercial AI products. While vendors market generative systems as autonomous intelligence, large language models rely heavily on large, low-wage human workforces to manually tag data, sort training sets, and remove illicit content. Finally, the panelists emphasize that despite the focus on sophisticated AI threats and zero-day exploits, real-world intrusions continue to exploit fundamental security gaps. Referencing a live TV hacking demonstration, panelists note that threat actors frequently succeed through weak or reused credentials and uninventoried external assets rather than complex exploit chains.

Key Takeaways:
Enterprises should direct AI and automation investments toward Tier-1 SOC log filtering, alert deduplication, and telemetry anomaly detection rather than unproven generative tools. Security teams must prioritize core security hygiene—comprehensive asset inventory and robust credential management—since basic oversights remain the primary vector for successful breaches. Vulnerability research and defense still depend on human analytical judgment to detect logic flaws that automated tools miss.

## Overview

In this presentation, speakers Lorin Wu and Porot Mo (with co-author Jack Tang noted as absent) introduce an automated approach for constructing a Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures (TTP) Knowledge Graph to generate adaptive attack paths for Breach and Attack Simulation (BAS) systems. 

Modern BAS platforms face three key requirements:
1. Continuously keeping pace with evolving adversary TTPs.
2. Selecting appropriate TTP simulations tailored to the target organization's actual operational environment.
3. Generating adaptive attack paths to evaluate and support defensive-in-depth postures.

To address these needs, the proposed framework consists of two core components: automated extraction of TTPs and associated artifacts from cyberattack reports to build a comprehensive TTP Knowledge Graph, and semantic reasoning over that graph to generate adaptive attack paths based on the target organization's specific context.

---

## TTP Extraction & NLP Methodology

The presenters evaluate prior and baseline extraction methods, observing limitations:
- **Trend Project:** Used traditional machine learning to extract TTPs, resulting in poor performance.
- **Threat-to-IOC / NER Task Models:** Identified words related to techniques using Named Entity Recognition (NER), but failed to identify the specific technique IDs and tactic names.
- **ChatGPT (OpenAI GPT-3.5):** Tested on May 5th using question prompts. The presenters noted that GPT-3.5 achieved a lower F1-score than their specialized TTP extractor.

To optimize TTP extraction accuracy, the authors implemented three primary enhancements:
1. **Primary vs. Secondary Technique Distinction:** Differentiates primary from secondary techniques to handle uneven sample distributions across training data.
2. **Multi-Perspective Extraction via NER:** Recognizes entities (tools, malware, command-line arguments, code snippets) using NER and infers associated TTPs based on entity relationships.
3. **N-gram Sliding Windows & Transfer Learning:** Uses N-gram sliding window resolution on attack descriptions paired with pre-trained Transformer language models. For Chinese-language materials, they applied Chinese word tokenization based on Whole Word Masking (WWM) and performed double-training / transfer learning for TTP extraction.

---

## TTP Knowledge Graph Construction

The extracted intelligence is modeled into a graph schema incorporating MITRE ATT&CK, playbooks, National Vulnerability Database (NVD) data, and PCAP datasets:
- **Techniques & Assets:** Maps dependencies between techniques and target asset states (e.g., Remote Desktop Protocol [RDP] requires a Windows OS platform with the RDP service running).
- **Techniques & Permissions:** Captures execution prerequisites (permissions required to execute a technique) and outcomes (privileges obtained post-execution).
- **Data Sources & Defensive Products:** Integrates MITRE ATT&CK detection data sources and maps them to enterprise security controls based on Security Operations Center (SOC) operational telemetry (e.g., associating EDR sensors with Windows registry event telemetry).
- **Playbooks & Vulnerabilities:** Links specific adversary procedures to attack playbooks, which are then tied to vulnerable assets, CVE/NVD vulnerability data, and packet capture network patterns.

---

## Adaptive Attack Path Reasoning for BAS

To ensure repeatability and realistic simulation, the system ingests concrete target environment data before executing reasoning:
- **Asset Information:** Target operating systems, running web services, host configurations, and installed software status.
- **Network Topology:** Zone locations and boundaries of assets across organizational segments, such as DMZ, internal office networks, and cloud environments.
- **Security Posture & Controls:** Environmental controls and defenses deployed across network segments.

By reasoning across asset dependencies, required/granted permissions, and topological placement stored within the Knowledge Graph, the system computes context-aware, adaptive attack paths tailored to the organization's defensive architecture.

Overview:
John Yolman, a security researcher at Elastic and former 15-year veteran of the Australian Signals Directorate, presents a defensive analysis of Windows memory scanning and evasive shellcode techniques. Yolman details how operating system hardening in 64-bit Windows inadvertently made private executable memory an indefensible boundary for security products. The talk explores memory protection fluctuation techniques introduced by Gargoyle in 2017 and outlines methodologies for detecting the subtle footprints left by dormant shellcode.

Key Topics:
- Windows 64-bit kernel hardening (PatchGuard, Driver Signing Enforcement, VBS) and the loss of private memory inspection
- State-of-the-art open-source memory scanners: Yara (signatures), Moneta (metadata anomalies), and Pe-sieve (hybrid heuristics)
- Memory protection fluctuation mechanics: Using timers, ROP gadgets, and dormant non-executable states (RW/NA)
- Detection strategies and hunting methodologies for identifying shellcode footprints in memory and thread artifacts

Technical Details:
Yolman reviews the evolution of Windows security architecture since 64-bit Windows Vista and Windows 10. Microsoft significantly hardened the kernel by introducing PatchGuard (Kernel Patch Protection), Driver Signing Enforcement, and Virtualization-Based Security (VBS), eliminating kernel rootkits. However, this shift created an architectural blind spot: while security products receive kernel callbacks for image loading (LoadLibrary), they receive no inline kernel notifications when private memory is allocated via VirtualAlloc or modified via VirtualProtect. User-mode hooks are inherently unsuited to defend against malicious code operating at the same privilege level, hypervisor shadow hooks conflict with VBS, and mitigations like Arbitrary Code Guard (ACG) proved too restrictive for mainstream applications and fell into disuse.

As a result, defenders rely heavily on user-mode memory scanning. Yolman categorizes current scanning technology through three open-source tools: Yara (pattern and signature matching of memory bytes), Moneta (analyzing memory metadata anomalies and conflicting page permissions), and Pe-sieve (a hybrid scanner evaluating content heuristics and unbacked PE images). If an implant evades these three mechanisms, it can typically evade commercial Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) memory scanners.

Malware authors bypass these scanners using memory protection fluctuation techniques, first popularized by Josh Lospinoso's Gargoyle in 2017. Because scanning the vast 64-bit address space is computationally prohibitive and prone to false positives from benign applications (such as hex editors, disassemblers, and browsers holding threat intelligence text), scanners inspect only executable pages. Exploiting this, modern shellcode remains dormant 99.9% of the time, marking its memory pages as Read-Write (RW) or No-Access (NA). Using asynchronous timers (such as waitable timers) and Return-Oriented Programming (ROP) gadgets, the shellcode awakens periodically, toggles permissions to RX, executes its beacon tasks, restores non-executable permissions, and returns to sleep. Yolman explains that defenders must shift away from scanning raw memory pages and instead hunt for auxiliary artifacts—such as anomalous waitable timer objects, suspicious call stack frames, and unbacked thread origins.

Key Takeaways:
Periodic memory scanning focused solely on executable pages is ineffective against advanced implants employing protection fluctuation techniques. Full-address-space memory scanning is unfeasible in production environments due to severe false-positive rates generated by developer tools and web browsers. Defenders must enhance detection capabilities by monitoring secondary artifacts, including waitable timer queues, unbacked thread call stacks, and suspicious permission transition patterns.
